item.text:
Based on the text alone, the principal loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement problems are:

1. **Section 2(1)(A) — “single training run” is undefined.** A company could divide training among nominally separate runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, or successive fine-tuning stages and argue that no individual run exceeded \(10^{26}\) operations.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — the threshold excludes systems at exactly \(10^{26}\) operations.** Because the definition says “greater than” rather than “equal to or greater than,” a run at precisely the stated threshold is outside this prong.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — computation is not measured or attributed.** The bill does not say whether to count failed computations, data processing, architecture searches, reinforcement learning, fine-tuning, inference-time computation, or work performed on behalf of the developer by another entity.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “integer or floating-point operations” is technologically underdefined.** There is no method for converting operations of different precision or counting specialized, analog, optical, or future hardware, allowing technically equivalent training to fall outside the stated metric.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — only a “model” trained above the threshold is covered.** A system assembled from multiple smaller models, none individually above the threshold, could collectively have the capabilities the legislation targets without satisfying this prong.

6. **Section 2(1)(B) — “the Secretary” is not identified.** The act never defines that term; because Section 6 separately refers to the “Secretary of State,” it is unclear whether Section 2 means the Secretary of Commerce or another official.

7. **Section 2(1)(B) — the capability standard is vague.** “Capable,” “substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” have no benchmarks, comparison population, testing conditions, or evidentiary standards, making classifications unpredictable and vulnerable to a vagueness challenge.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — coverage may depend on an affirmative agency determination.** A highly capable system arguably remains outside this prong until the Secretary formally determines that it qualifies, allowing continued work during agency delay, testing, or litigation.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — no determination process is provided.** The bill supplies no testing authority, notice procedure, deadline, evidentiary standard, appeal process, or mechanism for revisiting a determination after a system changes.

10. **Sections 2(1) and 3 — “model” and “system” are not distinguished.** It is unclear whether changing a model’s software wrapper, tools, data access, weights, or component models creates a new covered system or merely modifies an existing one.

11. **Section 2(2) — the definition of “U.S. person” is unusually narrow.** It omits permanent residents, other individuals subject to U.S. jurisdiction, partnerships, unincorporated associations, and entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law.

12. **Section 2(2) — foreign subsidiaries are not clearly U.S. persons.** A U.S. corporation could conduct work through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary, and the text does not address control, beneficial ownership, direction, financing, or assistance by the U.S. parent.

13. **Section 2(3) — “advanced AI chips” is undefined.** The facility threshold therefore lacks a technical performance standard and may not cover custom accelerators, older chips used in large numbers, non-chip computing hardware, or future architectures.

14. **Section 2(3) — the threshold can be avoided by distributing hardware.** A company could divide more than 50,000 chips among several nominal data centers, colocations, or neighboring facilities, because “data center” and facility boundaries are not defined.

15. **Section 2(3) — facilities with exactly 50,000 chips are excluded.** The definition applies only when a data center contains “more than” 50,000, and it does not address temporarily removed, inactive, leased, or remotely pooled chips.

16. **Section 2(3) and Section 4 — the registry’s geographic scope is unclear.** “Covered facility” is not limited to the United States, potentially imposing registration on foreign facilities while providing no clear jurisdictional basis for doing so.

17. **Section 3(a) — the prohibited acts are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” could be disputed at their margins, particularly for fine-tuning, testing, hosting, modifying, operating, or integrating a third party’s model.

18. **Section 3(a) — important enabling conduct is not expressly prohibited.** The provision does not clearly reach financing, selling, licensing, exporting, transferring weights, supplying computing resources, possessing, acquiring, or assisting with a covered system.

19. **Section 3(a) — the territorial language is ambiguous.** “Any person in the United States” could refer either to a person’s location or to where the conduct occurs, leaving uncertainty about remote work, cross-border cloud services, and conduct partly performed in the United States.

20. **Section 3(a) — responsibility in multi-party development is unclear.** The bill does not allocate liability among model creators, cloud providers, customers, open-source contributors, contractors, and downstream deployers.

21. **Section 3(b) — the grandfather clause is extremely broad.** If training began before enactment, the system is exempt not merely from the training ban but apparently from the prohibitions on later development and deployment as well.

22. **Section 3(b) — companies can establish grandfathered status with a token start.** The bill sets no minimum amount or continuity of pre-enactment training, so initiating a nominal run before enactment could support a claim to permanent exemption.

23. **Section 3(b) — the identity of a grandfathered system is undefined.** The text does not say when retraining, scaling, fine-tuning, changing architecture, adding tools, or releasing a successor turns an exempt existing system into a new covered system.

24. **Section 3(c) — the safety-evaluation exception has no safeguards.** It requires no advance approval, independent supervision, reporting, containment, time limit, compute limit, or prohibition on retaining and later using the resulting system.

25. **Section 3(c) — “for the purpose of” creates a subjective, potentially broad defense.** A company could characterize capability work or even deployment as safety evaluation, especially where an activity has both safety and commercial or developmental purposes.

26. **Section 3 generally — breadth and vagueness could impair enforcement.** The combination of an open-ended capability test and undefined prohibited activities is especially vulnerable in criminal cases, where due-process rules demand clearer notice of what conduct is illegal.

27. **Section 4(a) — “operator” is undefined.** Ownership, physical control, leasing, cloud management, and colocation arrangements may point to different operators, allowing each participant to argue that another party has the registration duty.

28. **Section 4(a) — no registration deadline or updating requirement is supplied.** The bill does not say when a facility must register, what information registration must contain, or whether changes in ownership, location, or chip count must be reported.

29. **Section 4(b) — workload reporting is too vague to ensure useful disclosure.** “Describing the computing workloads” specifies no format, level of detail, compute-accounting method, customer identification, retention period, or treatment of encrypted or proprietary workloads.

30. **Section 4(b) — certification is not backed by verification powers.** The bill provides no audit, inspection, monitoring, recordkeeping, subpoena, or chip-tracking authority with which Commerce could check an operator’s reports.

31. **Sections 4 and 5 — registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so failing to register, failing to report, or submitting an inaccurate report is not expressly subject to the act’s civil or criminal penalties.

32. **Sections 3–5 — no agency is expressly charged with enforcement.** The bill does not identify who may investigate violations, assess civil penalties, bring actions, seek injunctions, issue regulations, or order an unlawful system shut down.

33. **Section 5(a) — the civil penalty supplies little assessment guidance.** It provides only a maximum, with no minimum, penalty factors, administrative procedure, limitations period, or explanation of whether each system, entity, or act constitutes a separate violation.

34. **Section 5(a) — the “each day” rule is difficult to apply to discrete conduct.** Training or deployment may occur intermittently or instantaneously, and the bill does not say when a violation begins or ends or whether continued possession or availability counts as an ongoing violation.

35. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — the penalty dates conflict.** Section 5 purports to cover violations on or after enactment, but the act—including Section 3—does not take effect until 180 days later; attempting to penalize conduct during that interval would raise fair-notice and retroactivity problems.

36. **Section 5(b) — “willfully” creates a substantial criminal-proof burden.** Depending on its interpretation, prosecutors may have to show that a defendant knew the conduct violated the law, which will be difficult amid the bill’s undefined thresholds and exceptions.

37. **Section 5(b) — corporate and individual liability is not allocated.** The bill does not specify when executives, employees, contractors, or corporate entities are criminally responsible for organizational decisions.

38. **Section 6 — the international provision requires only an attempt.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate” an agreement, but need not conclude one, obtain equivalent foreign laws, report failure, or impose consequences if negotiations go nowhere.

39. **Section 6 — “equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** There is no standard for comparing foreign thresholds, exceptions, enforcement mechanisms, or penalties, and no designated decision-maker for determining equivalence.

40. **Section 7(a) — the National Academies report process is incomplete.** The bill neither directs the Academies to produce a report nor provides a deadline, criteria, funding, required findings, or a procedure for Congress to receive and act on it.

41. **Section 7(a) — termination by joint resolution lacks procedural detail.** No expedited process is provided, and the text does not specify the required language or clarify that the resolution must complete bicameral passage and presentment.

42. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — the two termination provisions do not fit cleanly together.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes a safety finding, while Section 7(b) ends the entire act after ten years regardless of any finding; the sunset therefore defeats the ostensibly safety-based duration rule.

43. **Section 7(b) — the sunset may terminate unresolved obligations and enforcement.** The act does not preserve accrued penalties, pending cases, reporting records, or investigations after the ten-year date.

44. **Sections 5–8 — no transition rules are provided.** The text does not address training begun during the 180-day delay, facilities that cross the chip threshold near the effective date, or systems subject to an ongoing investigation when the act sunsets.

45. **Act-wide — no rulemaking authority is expressly granted.** Commerce lacks a clear delegation to define technical terms, prescribe reports, update obsolete compute or chip thresholds, or close avoidance strategies as technology changes.

46. **Act-wide — no severability clause is included.** If a court invalidates a central definition, the Secretary’s classification authority, or the prohibition, the absence of severability language could increase uncertainty over whether the remainder can operate independently.

47. **Act-wide — the bill supplies no resources or appropriations.** It creates classification, registry, reporting, diplomatic, and enforcement responsibilities without authorizing staffing or funding, increasing the risk of delayed determinations and weak oversight.
